The local bus from Kheri to the polytechnic in Sirsa rattled over every pothole, and Jasleen kept her phone face down on her knee. Rajni reached over and turned it up. The class group again: Jasleen's photo from the field visit, mud on her chappals, captioned 'Village Queen arrives', with forty laughing reactions under it.
'Arre, it's just masti,' Rajni said. 'They tease everyone in first year.'
Jasleen looked out at the mustard fields. 'You say masti, so I'm supposed to smile. I've eaten lunch behind the workshop for a week so they can't see me.'
Rajni's thumb stopped over the screen. One of the forty reactions was hers.
'They're mocking you,' she said slowly, 'and it's hurting you.'
She took back her reaction, then typed in the group: 'Not funny. Stop.'

qa.q: Where has Jasleen been eating lunch for the past week?
qa.a: Jasleen has eaten lunch behind the workshop for a week so they can't see her.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's face-down phone suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she dreads seeing the group; she feels ashamed and wants to hide from the jokes, not laugh along with them.

qa.q: Which choice of Rajni's changed things on the bus, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Rajni stopped calling it masti, said plainly that they were mocking Jasleen and it was hurting her, then took back her reaction and posted 'Not funny. Stop.'; naming it let Jasleen's hurt count.

qa.q: What might Rajni feel on noticing that one of the forty reactions was her own?
qa.a: Rajni probably feels a jolt of guilt, realising she had been part of the crowd that made the joke look harmless while Jasleen was eating alone.

grounding: A student whose mockery in the class group is waved off as masti tells a friend what it really costs her, and the friend names it plainly.

passage:
Pallavi joined the quarterly call from a crowded local train, one bar of signal, eleven minutes before her stop. Uday, the operations head, was sharing a slide: 'Rightsizing the Nashik warehouse to optimise headcount.'
The picture froze. By the time the audio came back, he was already on the next slide.
Pallavi unmuted, a vendor shouting 'chai, chai' behind her. 'Uday, sorry, before we move on. In plain words: how many people lose their jobs, and who tells them?'
A pause. 'Twenty-two loaders. HR will email them on Friday.'
The chat box, silent all call, filled up. 'Email?' 'Some of them don't check email.' 'Can they hear it in person?'
Uday rubbed his forehead. 'Fair. I'll go to Nashik on Thursday and talk to them with HR. Pallavi, send me the questions you'd want answered if it were you.'
Her station came. She typed the list standing by the door.

qa.q: How many loaders at the Nashik warehouse were losing their jobs?
qa.a: Twenty-two loaders, and HR planned to email them on Friday.

qa.q: What did Pallavi want the call to notice when she unmuted despite the noise?
qa.a: She wanted everyone to see the actual people behind 'rightsizing', worried that the slide would move on before anyone asked who was affected and how.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the call, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Pallavi's plain question was the turning point; once Uday said 'twenty-two loaders' and 'email', others spoke up, and Uday chose to go to Nashik and tell them face to face.

qa.q: How might the twenty-two loaders be affected by the way the call went?
qa.a: Instead of learning by an email some might not even check, they will hear it in person with HR there to answer questions; the loss still hurts, but they are treated as people.

grounding: An employee hears a layoff called rightsizing and asks plainly how many people lose jobs and who tells them, which turns the meeting's attention to them.

At six in the morning, the central kitchen in Kochi smelled of onions and steam. Simran, the new floor manager, pinned a chart by the walk-in fridge: 'Motivation Wall: slowest three packers of the day.'
'It's just to push everyone a little,' she said, smiling. 'Healthy pressure.'
Maria, who had packed lunches here for four years, dried her hands. 'Can I ask what it does, exactly? Whose names go up, and then what?'
Simran blinked. 'The bottom three. They stay back to clean.'
'So Latha, who's slow because of her wrist, and the two boys who joined last week. Every day. In front of the delivery riders.'
Simran looked at the chart for a long moment. Latha was already at the sink, head down.
'I didn't think of it as names,' Simran said quietly. She unpinned it. 'Let's rotate the cleaning instead. And tell me who needs help getting faster.'

qa.q: What did Simran call the chart she pinned by the walk-in fridge?
qa.a: She called it the 'Motivation Wall', for the slowest three packers of the day.

qa.q: Why did the chart seem reasonable to Simran at first?
qa.a: Simran thought of it as healthy pressure that would push everyone a little; the word 'motivation' kept the real people, like Latha and the new boys, out of her mind.

qa.q: Which question changed Simran's decision, and why did it work?
qa.a: Maria's plain question, 'Whose names go up, and then what?'; it made Simran picture Latha and the new boys shamed every day, so she unpinned the chart and rotated the cleaning.

qa.q: What would it be like for Latha if the chart had stayed up?
qa.a: Latha would likely see her name on the wall almost every day in front of the riders, singled out for a wrist she cannot help; the 'motivation' would feel like public shame.

grounding: A worker hears pressure called motivation and asks exactly whose names go up and what happens to them, which makes the manager see the people.

Ojas, you said everyone in your class ignored the new boy, so it wasn't really you. Let me tell you about Bhola.
In Class 5 in Jabalpur, Bhola's father sold milk, and his shirt smelled of the cowshed. One morning a boy in the assembly line held his nose, and soon the whole line did. I held mine too. It felt like a game. For weeks nobody walked to school with Bhola.
When my Amma found out, I said, 'Everyone was doing it!'
She asked, 'Then how much of it was yours, Harish?'
I said, 'Only a little.'
'And Bhola,' she said, 'did he get only a little hurt?'
The next day I walked beside him. Two other boys followed.
So, Ojas, what part of today was yours?

qa.q: What did the boys in the assembly line do to Bhola that morning?
qa.a: One boy held his nose at Bhola, and soon the whole line did, Harish included.

qa.q: Why did holding the nose feel acceptable to young Harish at the time?
qa.a: Because the whole line was doing it, it felt like a game and only 'a little' Harish's fault; being one of many made the act feel shared and small.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Harish, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Amma's question, whether Bhola got 'only a little hurt', was the turning point; the next day Harish chose to walk beside Bhola, and two other boys followed.

qa.q: How might Bhola have experienced those weeks, compared with how the boys saw them?
qa.a: To the boys it was a shared game with each doing only a little, but Bhola walked to school alone every day and carried the whole weight of it.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a whole line in shunning a classmate and claiming everyone was doing it, showing how a shared act feels like no one's fault.

Rain hammered the tin roof, so Class 6B was stuck inside for recess. Nikhita drew a chalk square on the floor: 'Secret club. Members only.' Eight girls squeezed in. When Mehak came over with her ludo board, Nikhita said, 'Full.' Then she looked at Disha. 'Right, Disha?'
Disha glanced at the others. Everyone was nodding. 'Full,' she repeated.
Mehak sat alone by the dripping window, lining up ludo pieces nobody would move.
Later, Ms Rao asked the club what had happened. 'I only said one word,' Disha said. 'Everyone else said it first.'
'Eight people, one word each,' Ms Rao said. 'How many words did Mehak hear?'
Disha counted on her fingers and stopped at eight. She looked over at the window.

qa.q: What did Mehak bring over to the chalk square?
qa.a: Mehak came over with her ludo board.

qa.q: Why did saying 'Full' feel small to Disha?
qa.a: Disha felt it was only one word and everyone else had said it first, so the blame seemed spread across the whole group rather than resting on her.

qa.q: When Disha looks over at the window, what choice could she make next?
qa.a: Disha could go and play ludo with Mehak or tell the club there is room; one person stepping out of the group can start to undo those eight words.

qa.q: What was recess like for Mehak by the dripping window?
qa.a: Mehak heard 'Full' from the whole group and spent recess alone lining up pieces; to her it felt like being turned away eight times, not once. 😔

grounding: A child who joins a group in shutting a classmate out says everyone else said it first, as if the shared act belonged to no one.

Subject: About the photo of Ira

Dear Mrs Fernandes,
You asked me to write down what happened, so here it is.
On Tuesday at the science fair, Tamanna took a photo of Ira mid-sneeze, braces showing, glasses slipping. Tamanna is house captain, and she said, 'Send it to the Class 10 group, it's hilarious.' So I sent it. I didn't take it and I didn't write the caption. I only forwarded it because she told me to.
I know Ira didn't come to school on Wednesday or Thursday. But I think Tamanna and the forty people who reacted should be asked about that too, not only me.
Honestly, when a house captain tells you something, you don't really argue.
I keep checking whether Ira has seen the group.
Aadhya, 10B

qa.q: According to Aadhya, who gave the instruction to send the photo?
qa.a: Tamanna, the house captain, who said, 'Send it to the Class 10 group, it's hilarious.'

qa.q: Why does forwarding the photo feel reasonable to Aadhya from the inside?
qa.a: Aadhya feels uneasy, still checking whether Ira has seen the group, but since Tamanna took the photo and gave the order, Aadhya's own part feels like just going along.

qa.q: What choice could Aadhya make now that would actually help Ira?
qa.a: Aadhya could own the one step that was Aadhya's, pressing send, then ask the group to delete the photo and apologise to Ira directly.

qa.q: How might Ira see the question of who 'only' forwarded the photo?
qa.a: For Ira it hardly matters who took it or who gave the order; every forward spread the sneeze photo further, and Ira stayed away from school for two days after it.

grounding: A teenager who spread an embarrassing photo writes that the house captain told them to send it, placing the responsibility on the person in charge.

The only signal in Hansa's village came near the water tank behind the panchayat office, so that's where she stood at dusk, phone held high. The college group had 212 members, and tonight it was all about Arohi's speech from English Day: a still of her mid-word, mouth wide, with new captions pasted on it every few minutes: 'Me explaining responsibility to my goat.' 'Arohi when the mic is on.'
Laughing faces, then more. Hansa scrolled. Surely Manpreet, the class rep, would say something. Or one of the toppers. Someone.
Twenty minutes passed. Nobody did. Another caption appeared.
Her mother called from the courtyard that the rotis were getting cold.
Hansa typed, deleted, typed again: 'Arohi practised this for a week. It's not funny to me. Please stop.'
She sent it and went in to eat. When she came back to the tank, Manpreet had written, 'Hansa's right. Enough.' Below it, the first poster had typed, 'Sorry, Arohi. Took it too far.'

qa.q: Where does Hansa go to get signal in her village?
qa.a: She goes near the water tank behind the panchayat office.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking during the twenty minutes of scrolling?
qa.a: Hansa felt hesitant and kept expecting someone else, Manpreet the class rep or one of the toppers, to speak up; with 212 members it felt as if it could not be her job.

qa.q: Which choice changed the group chat, and why did it work?
qa.a: Hansa's short, calm message naming Arohi's effort and asking the group to stop; once one person spoke, Manpreet backed it up and the first poster apologised to Arohi.

qa.q: What might the evening have been like for Arohi before and after Hansa's message?
qa.a: Before, Arohi would have watched laughing faces pile up with nobody on her side; after, she could see Hansa and Manpreet stand up for her and read an apology from the poster.

Monday's statistics lecture at the university in Toronto was online because of a snowstorm, ninety-three students in little boxes. Fatima's camera switched on by accident while she was eating soup, and before she noticed, someone had taken a screenshot.
The side chat lit up: 'soup queen', a slurping sound effect, the screenshot again.
Mateo watched from his kitchen table. The TA is in this call, he thought. Somebody will say something. He waited through two slides. The jokes kept coming, and Fatima's box went black.
He unmuted, heart thumping, and kept his voice level. 'Hey, can we drop the screenshot? Anyone's camera could do that. Let's get back to the slides.'
A second of silence. Then the TA: 'Thanks, Mateo. Please delete it.' A few messages appeared: 'yeah, sorry.'
After class, Mateo messaged Fatima: 'That was rough. You okay?'

qa.q: What was Fatima doing when her camera switched on by accident?
qa.a: She was eating soup.

qa.q: Why did Mateo wait through two slides before speaking?
qa.a: Mateo felt hesitant, assuming the TA or somebody among the ninety-three would deal with it; with so many people watching, it felt as if it was not his job.

qa.q: What choice did Mateo make, and how did it change the call?
qa.a: He chose to unmute and calmly ask everyone to drop the screenshot, noting anyone's camera could do that; the TA backed him and others apologised.

qa.q: If you were Fatima, what would Mateo's message after class mean to you?
qa.a: It would show that at least one person saw how awful the moment was and cared; after the jokes, a simple 'You okay?' could make it feel less lonely. 🤍

grounding: A student in a large online class waits for someone else to stop a pile-on, then speaks up calmly himself and others follow.

Monday: Sudha found it at 7 p.m. The school-fees portal charged some parents twice if they pressed 'pay' on a slow connection. Tanvir, her manager, read the ticket and said, 'Mark it low priority. The client demo is Thursday. We'll patch it quietly after launch.'
Tuesday: Sudha had barely slept. At the morning stand-up she said, 'I understand why you want it that way, Tanvir. But I'm the one signing off on testing, and I can't sign that it's safe. I'm logging it as critical and raising it with the quality lead today.' Tanvir's jaw tightened. 'Your call.'
Friday: The launch had moved by one week. The quality lead thanked Sudha in the team channel. Tanvir stopped by her desk, a little awkward. 'The client said they'd rather wait than refund two hundred parents.'
'I know,' Sudha said. 'Thanks for not stopping me.'

qa.q: What did the fees portal do when parents pressed 'pay' on a slow connection?
qa.a: It charged some parents twice.

qa.q: Why had Sudha barely slept on Monday night?
qa.a: She felt torn: she understood Tanvir's deadline, but she felt the sign-off was her own responsibility and knew parents would be charged twice if she stayed quiet.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why was the way Sudha raised it wise?
qa.a: At Tuesday's stand-up Sudha said openly that she understood the instruction but could not sign it off, then took it to the quality lead that day; using the proper channel let the company fix it before launch.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Sudha's choice by Friday?
qa.a: Tanvir was tense on Tuesday, but by Friday seems relieved and a little embarrassed, having learned the client preferred a short delay to refunding two hundred parents.

grounding: An employee told to hide a defect says she understands the instruction but stays accountable for her sign-off, and raises it with the quality lead.

You asked me, Pooja, what I'd do if a boss told me to hide something. I'll tell you what I did do, at twenty-five, in the dyeing unit at Tiruppur.
A lot of four thousand children's T-shirts bled colour in the wash test. The export deadline was two days away. Mr Raghavan, my supervisor, said, 'Vasudha, just write "pass". The buyer never tests again.'
I was scared. He had hired me. I said, 'Sir, I understand why you're asking. But my initials go on that sheet, not yours. I can't write something false.' That evening I sent the report to the compliance manager, as our rulebook said.
The shipment was late by ten days. Mr Raghavan didn't speak to me for a week. Then one morning he left the new test sheets on my desk and said, 'You sign these.'
Bosses give orders, Pooja. Your pen is still yours.

qa.q: How many T-shirts were in the lot that failed the wash test?
qa.a: Four thousand children's T-shirts.

qa.q: What was young Vasudha feeling when Mr Raghavan asked for a 'pass', and why?
qa.a: Vasudha was scared of crossing the supervisor who had done the hiring, yet still felt personally answerable, because Vasudha's initials would go on the sheet.

qa.q: Which choice did Vasudha make, and why was it a sound one?
qa.a: Vasudha politely refused to write 'pass' and that evening sent the report to the compliance manager as the rulebook said; it kept the record honest through the proper route rather than a quiet fight.

qa.q: How did Mr Raghavan's view of Vasudha seem to change over time?
qa.a: At first he was annoyed enough to stay silent for a week, but later he trusted Vasudha with the new test sheets, which suggests he came to respect the refusal.

grounding: An elder recalls being told by a supervisor to pass a faulty lot, refusing because the signature was their own, and reporting it through the proper channel.

passage:
I'm Jagdish, and last summer in our railway colony I had a rule: no playing with the Line kids. They lived in the huts by the tracks, and I told everyone they were jungli and dirty. So when their ball bounced into our lane, I kicked it into the drain. 'They're used to muck,' I said. 'They won't mind.'
My cousin Preeti fished it out and walked it back to them. I was angry with her.
The next day I saw a girl from the huts, Sulochana, crying by the drain and washing that ball with her hands. It was her birthday ball, Preeti told me.
I didn't feel like a winner. I felt small.
Now I say their names. Sulochana bowls better than me.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do with the ball when it bounced into the lane?
qa.a: Jagdish kicked it into the drain.

qa.q: Why did kicking the ball away feel okay to Jagdish at that moment?
qa.a: Jagdish had been calling the Line kids jungli and dirty, so they seemed not to feel things the same way; 'they won't mind' made the unkind act feel harmless.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jagdish, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Seeing Sulochana crying and washing her birthday ball; Jagdish felt small, dropped the 'jungli' label and started using the children's names.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen the Line kids differently from Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti treated them as ordinary children whose ball mattered, so she fished it out and took it back; to her they were simply neighbours.

grounding: A child who calls the children from the huts dirty and wild treats their things roughly, until seeing one girl's tears makes her a person again.

Coach's note, Saturday junior football, Old City ground. Noor.
Hafsa (9) refused to join a mixed team today. 'Not with the Kaman Gali lot. They're wild. They bite.' When I paired her with Mehrunnisa from that lane, Hafsa pulled the yellow bib off Mehrunnisa's shoulders and said, 'She doesn't need it, they play like goats anyway.' Two of her friends laughed.

qa.q: What choice did Coach Noor make after stopping the drill, and why did it help?
qa.a: Noor chose not to lecture but had each child say one thing about their partner; hearing Mehrunnisa praise her left foot led Hafsa to see and name a real person.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have felt like for Mehrunnisa?
qa.a: Mehrunnisa was called a goat and had her bib pulled off in front of others, which likely stung, yet she still said something generous about Hafsa.

grounding: A coach notes a child who calls children from another lane wild and treats one roughly, and helps her see one of them as a person.

Youth group note, parish hall, Margao. Reena (leader).
Friday. During the snack break, Joseph (15) had the group laughing about the workers building the new flats next door: 'They're donkeys, na? Twenty of them in one room, can't even read a sign.' He made braying noises when one of them walked past the gate. Two younger boys copied him.
I noticed he never used a single name. When I asked whether he knew any of them, he shrugged: 'They're all the same.'
What I did: on Sunday I asked the site supervisor if one of the workers would share lunch with us. Dinesh came, from a village two days away by train, and passed round a photo of his daughter's school certificate. Joseph asked him three questions and didn't bray once.
Plan: Joseph has offered to help with the Sunday reading class for the workers' children. I'll check in with him about how it goes.

qa.q: What sound did Joseph make when a worker walked past the gate?
qa.a: He made braying noises.

qa.q: Why did the jokes feel harmless to Joseph at the time?
qa.a: Joseph felt amused, seeing the workers as 'all the same', a faceless crowd rather than people, so mocking them felt like a laugh rather than cruelty.

qa.q: Which step of Reena's changed Joseph's behaviour, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Dinesh to share lunch; once Joseph met one real person with a name and a daughter's certificate, the braying stopped and questions took its place.

qa.q: What would change for the two younger boys if Reena had not stepped in?
qa.a: They would likely learn that mocking the workers wins laughs, and keep seeing the people next door as animals rather than neighbours.

grounding: A youth leader notes a teenager who calls a group of workers donkeys and never names them, and how meeting one of them changes things.

Thursday, 9:40 p.m.
Inter-school quiz today. The government school team sat across from us in the hall, and at the break Mitali said, 'Look, the buffalo herd has arrived.' I added, 'Mooing the answers, probably,' and our whole bench cracked up. I kept the mooing going all lunch. It was honestly funny.
Then they beat us in the final round. Their captain, Sunaina, got the one about monsoon winds before I'd even touched the buzzer.
At the handshake she said, 'Good match, Nandini,' because she'd read my name tag. I didn't know hers until the announcer said it.
I can't stop thinking about that. She looked at me like a person, and all day I'd been making cow noises at her.
Not writing any more tonight.

qa.q: Who answered the question about monsoon winds?
qa.a: Sunaina, the captain of the government school team.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nandini feels uneasy and ashamed: the entry says Nandini 'can't stop thinking' about Sunaina using a name after a day of cow noises, and it ends abruptly.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nandini's day, and what could Nandini do now?
qa.a: The handshake, when Sunaina used Nandini's name; Nandini could drop the mooing jokes and learn the names of the other team's players.

qa.q: How might the lunch-break jokes have looked from the government school bench?
qa.a: They may have heard a whole bench mooing at them and felt dismissed as a herd, not seen as a quiz team, which they then proved in the final round.

grounding: A teenager who joins jokes calling another school's team a buffalo herd is shaken when one of them greets the teenager by name.

passage:
In my first winter in Dublin, I was a number more often than a name. At the immigration office I was 'fifty-eight'. At the accommodation desk I was 'another non-EU one', said to a colleague as if I couldn't hear. A tutor once sighed that international students 'take up all the help'. I started keeping my coat on in seminars, as if I might be asked to leave.
What pulled me back was small. My lab partner Thomas said 'Morning, Noor' every single day, and asked what I thought about the results before he wrote anything down. On Sundays I called my cousin in Lucknow, who laughed at all my stories.
I still flinch when I hear 'fifty-eight'. But I learned to spend more of my time with the people who say my name.

qa.q: What number was Noor called at the immigration office?
qa.a: Fifty-eight.

qa.q: What does keeping a coat on in seminars suggest about how Noor felt?
qa.a: It suggests Noor felt unwelcome and temporary, like a burden who might be asked to leave, rather than a student who belonged.

qa.q: What choice helped Noor through that winter?
qa.a: Noor chose to spend more time with people who used Noor's name, Thomas in the lab and the cousin on Sunday calls; those ties pushed back against feeling like a number.

qa.q: How might Thomas's daily 'Morning, Noor' have looked from Thomas's side?

Joseph, second-year B.Com, from Aizawl, came in after the fee office sent him back a third time. The clerk calls him '4127' and told him in front of the queue, 'You outside students are always a headache.' He said the mess manager does the same: 'Next plate, next plate,' never a name.

I used his name while we talked, and asked about home. He smiled for the first time when he described his mother's shop.
Next steps: I walked with him to the fee office and spoke to the clerk myself. He agreed to try football again on Friday; his classmate Lalrin plays there. Follow-up next Wednesday.

I'm Ranjana. Last month at the team lunch, Gulnaz rolled her eyes about the new interns from the small-town colleges. 'Copy-paste machines. No brains, no English, just attendance.' People laughed. I almost did.
Instead I asked, 'Which one? Tell me about one of them.'
Gulnaz paused. 'Well... Mohit, the tall one.'
'What's Mohit like?'
'He comes in at eight because the bus from his village is the only one.' She stirred her dal. 'He asked me how to write a proper email. Twice.'
'Did he get it right the second time?'
She almost smiled. 'Better than some of us.'
The next week I saw her at Mohit's desk, going through his draft line by line. I think about that often. The whole group was easy to sneer at. One boy with a bus timetable wasn't.

qa.q: Why does Mohit come in at eight?
qa.a: Because the bus from his village is the only one.

qa.q: Why did Gulnaz's contempt seem to soften during the lunch?
qa.a: Talking about Mohit made her picture a real person who travels far and asked for help; she almost smiled, as if the sneer was harder to hold once she thought of him.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the lunch, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ranjana's question, 'Tell me about one of them', instead of laughing along; it moved Gulnaz from a sneer about a group to one person with a story.

qa.q: How might Mohit experience the change in Gulnaz the following week?
qa.a: Mohit now has a senior going through his draft line by line, which likely makes him feel noticed and helped rather than dismissed as a copy-paste machine.

grounding: An adult hears a group of interns described with contempt and asks about one of them, and the individual story brings back empathy.

Keerthana (24) sat in on Monday's meeting when the desk discussed the families near the canal who are being moved. A senior called them 'encroachers, the usual rent-seeking crowd', and the plan was a two-line brief.

Keerthana read her notes aloud at the evening meeting. The same senior asked, quietly, how far the new site was from the school.
We ran it as a full story with Bhagyamma's photo. I have asked Keerthana to lead the follow-up.

qa.a: Bhagyamma has lived by the canal for nineteen years.

qa.q: Which choice turned a two-line brief into a full story?
qa.a: Keerthana's choice to visit and listen to Bhagyamma, then read the notes aloud; one real face made the desk ask real questions, like how far the new site was from the school.

qa.q: What changed for the senior who used the word 'encroachers'?
qa.a: After hearing about Bhagyamma, the senior quietly asked how far the new site was from the school, a sign the contempt was giving way to concern for an actual family.
